extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, popular science, and internet culture
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and evaluating an online experiment (LaughLab) that solicited joke submissions and had users rate jokes to determine the 'world's funniest joke.' Focus is on the study's design, voting/selection method, and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-submitted joke archive (submission)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first section allowed users to submit their favorite joke to the archive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open submissions were accepted online; the study ultimately received a total of 40,000 joke submissions, indicating the archive was populated by voluntary user contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness rating scale
rubrics_metrics.description: "Users were asked to rate how funny they thought a selection of random jokes were on a scale from 'not very funny' to 'very funny.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participant ratings on this ordinal scale were the primary measure of a joke's funniness; these ratings, aggregated across users, determined top-ranked jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random selection of jokes for rating
rubrics_metrics.description: The site presented "a selection of random jokes" for users to rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using random selection of items for each rater is the study's sampling method intended to expose participants to a variety of jokes and reduce selection bias in which jokes are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity / vote-based ranking (top-rated gags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top jokes were identified by participant votes — the article refers to the study's "top-rated gags" and announces a winning gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate vote totals and mean ratings determined which jokes were ranked highest; the winning joke was the top-rated entry as judged by the voting population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large, international sample as legitimacy metric
rubrics_metrics.description: "Over 350,000 people from 70 countries participated, and close to 2 million votes were cast."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High participation and international reach are presented as evidence of the study's scale and generalizability; the study was later awarded the Guinness World Record for 'Largest internet joke vote.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/dissemination of results
rubrics_metrics.description: "A book containing all of the study’s results, as well as its top-rated gags, was also published in 2002."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing a compiled, published record (book) of results is an outcome metric and a way to validate and promulgate the study's findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance/originality of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that Wiseman "discovered a few years later that the joke’s origins could be traced back to a 1951 BBC sketch."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing a joke's origin highlights that top-rated jokes may be recycled or copied from earlier sources; originality is a relevant consideration when interpreting 'best/funniest' labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/therapeutic use of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner's submitter Gurpal Gosall "told Wiseman that he sometimes used the joke as a way of cheering up his patients," explaining it reminded them "that there were always people out there doing stupider things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond abstract funniness, a joke may be evaluated by its practical effect (e.g., cheering patients), suggesting usefulness or applicability is an evaluative dimension in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication / culturally scoped polls
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece references a 2010 OnePoll study seeking to find the best British jokes (voted on by 40,000 people) and The Telegraph's compilation of top 50 jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar polls with different samples or national scopes can yield different 'top' jokes; cultural context and sample composition are important when comparing results across studies.
